claim: The zebrafish (Danio rerio) has hundreds of NLR immune genes.
source: The zebrafish (Danio rerio) has hundreds of NLR immune genes, making this species ideal for studying this phenomenon.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about zebrafish.

claim: By sequencing 93 zebrafish from multiple wild and laboratory populations, a total of 1513 NLRs were identified.
source: By sequencing 93 zebrafish from multiple wild and laboratory populations, we identified a total of 1513 NLRs, many more than the previously known 400.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The previously known number of NLRs in zebrafish was 400.
source: By sequencing 93 zebrafish from multiple wild and laboratory populations, we identified a total of 1513 NLRs, many more than the previously known 400.
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge being compared to the new findings.

claim: Approximately half of the identified NLRs are present in all wild populations.
source: Approximately half of those are present in all wild populations, but only 4% were found in 80% or more of the individual fish.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis presented in the abstract.

claim: Only 4% of identified NLRs were found in 80% or more of the individual fish.
source: Approximately half of those are present in all wild populations, but only 4% were found in 80% or more of the individual fish.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis presented in the abstract.

claim: Wild fish have up to two times as many NLRs per individual as laboratory strains.
source: Wild fish have up to two times as many NLRs per individual and up to four times as many NLRs per population than laboratory strains.
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the data analysis presented in the abstract.

claim: Wild fish have up to four times as many NLRs per population as laboratory strains.
source: Wild fish have up to two times as many NLRs per individual and up to four times as many NLRs per population than laboratory strains.
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the data analysis presented in the abstract.

claim: Around half of the NLR gene copies are monomorphic.
source: In contrast to the massive variability of gene copies, nucleotide diversity in zebrafish NLR genes is very low: around half of the copies are monomorphic and the remaining ones have very few polymorphisms, likely a signature of purifying selection.
evidence: This is a finding from the nucleotide diversity analysis presented in the abstract.

claim: The remaining NLR gene copies that are not monomorphic have very few polymorphisms.
source: In contrast to the massive variability of gene copies, nucleotide diversity in zebrafish NLR genes is very low: around half of the copies are monomorphic and the remaining ones have very few polymorphisms, likely a signature of purifying selection.
evidence: This is a finding from the nucleotide diversity analysis presented in the abstract.

claim: The low nucleotide diversity in zebrafish NLR genes is likely a signature of purifying selection.
source: In contrast to the massive variability of gene copies, nucleotide diversity in zebrafish NLR genes is very low: around half of the copies are monomorphic and the remaining ones have very few polymorphisms, likely a signature of purifying selection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on evolutionary theory.

claim: Proteins containing a large nucleotide-binding domain followed by smaller repeats have an immune function in animals, plants, fungi, and bacteria.
source: In particular, proteins containing a large nucleotide-binding domain followed by smaller repeats have an immune function in animals, plants, fungi, and bacteria alike (Ting et al., 2008; Jones and Dangl, 2006; Uehling et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: In animals, the repeats in NLR proteins are usually leucine-rich repeats (LRRs).
source: In animals, these repeats are usually leucine-rich repeats (LRRs) and the proteins themselves are classified as NLRs (nucleotide binding domain leucine-rich repeat containing, also known as NOD-like receptors).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about NLR protein structure.

claim: Some NLRs act as pathogen sensors or transcription factors.
source: They have a multitude of functions: some act as pathogen sensors or transcription factors (Almeida-da-Silva et al., 2023), others are components or modulators of inflammasomes, large protein complexes that are assembled within cells as part of the response to biological or chemical danger (Almeida-da-Silva et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Some NLRs are components or modulators of inflammasomes.
source: They have a multitude of functions: some act as pathogen sensors or transcription factors (Almeida-da-Silva et al., 2023), others are components or modulators of inflammasomes, large protein complexes that are assembled within cells as part of the response to biological or chemical danger (Almeida-da-Silva et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Inflammasomes are large protein complexes that are assembled within cells as part of the response to biological or chemical danger.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Plants have their own NLRs that are structurally similar to the ones from animals.
source: Plants have their own NLRs that are structurally similar to the ones from animals and also carry out central functions in the immune response (Urbach and Ausubel, 2017; Yue et al., 2012).

claim: Plant NLRs carry out central functions in the immune response.
source: Plants have their own NLRs that are structurally similar to the ones from animals and also carry out central functions in the immune response (Urbach and Ausubel, 2017; Yue et al., 2012).

claim: NLR diversity has been extensively characterized in several plant species, including the thale cress (Arabidopsis thaliana).

claim: Vastly different NLR repertoires have been found from different strains or individuals of Arabidopsis thaliana.

source: The zebrafish reference genome contains nearly 400 NLR genes, two-thirds of which are located on the putative sex chromosome (chromosome 4), in a genomic region associated with extensive haplotypic variation (Howe et al., 2013; Howe et al., 2016; McConnell et al., 2023; Anderson et al., 2012).

source: By adapting and modifying a protocol that combines bait-based exon capture with PacBio SMRT technology (Witek et al., 2016), we successfully generated circular consensus sequence (CCS) data for targeted parts of the immune repertoire from 93 zebrafish (of initial 96), representing four wild populations (Figure 1B) and two laboratory strains.
